definition: Melodic means having a pleasant, tuneful quality, like music; characterized by a flowing melody.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word melodic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know melodic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Even the pigeons seemed to settle when the violinist began, her melodic phrases drifting across the plaza like a half-remembered song.
A sound can be merely pleasant without forming any real tune; melodic goes further, flowing like actual music.
Mellifluous—literally 'flowing with honey'—describes sound so sweetly smooth it goes beyond ordinary melodic quality.

Tuneful is the plainer, everyday word for a sound that carries a pleasing tune — a tuneful whistle, a tuneful jingle. Melodic is the slightly more formal term and points at the shape of the line, the smooth rise and fall of the melody. Reviews say melodic; a kid's happy humming is tuneful.

Musical is the broad word for anything involving or resembling music at all — musical talent, a musical family, a musical laugh. Melodic makes a narrower claim about the sound itself: it carries a flowing, pleasing tune. A child can be musical without singing a note; a sound is melodic only when it carries a melody.

Harmonious praises how separate notes or voices blend together at the same moment — a choir's chords, instruments in agreement. Melodic praises a single line's shape: the tune's own rise and fall. One voice alone can be melodic but never harmonious; a chord can be harmonious with no melody in it.
Discordant sounds clash unpleasantly instead of flowing like a tune.
A grating sound scrapes at the ears—the opposite of a smooth, pleasing melody.
The melodious call of the loon carried across the lake at dusk.
Melodic means having a pleasant, tuneful quality, like music; characterized by a flowing melody.
Kneading dough at dawn, Grandma Rosa hummed a low, melodic tune that rose and fell so smoothly the whole kitchen seemed to sway along.
The sentence describes an actual sound—a hummed tune with a smooth rise and fall—which is exactly what melodic means: pleasant and tuneful, like music.
Notice that melodic describes sound quality itself, not writing or ideas.
Use melodic for actual sound: voices, birdsong, instruments, ringtones.
It fits reviews, everyday talk, and descriptive writing alike.
Be careful not to borrow it for writing style—prose that flows beautifully is lyrical, not melodic.

The subway agency's new door-chime was two years in the making.
Its designers auditioned hundreds of three-note sequences before choosing one riders now hum on the platform.
The winning chime is unmistakably melodic: it rises, pauses, and settles, a tiny complete tune.
Engineers had pushed for a plain buzzer, which cuts through noise just as well.
But the agency's research found that a fragment of melody calms a crowded car in a way no buzz can, and the humming proved the point — riders had adopted the sound as a song.
